fields.Front: Describe the structure of an atom as Chapter 2 does, with the mass figures.
fields.Back: An extremely dense, positively charged nucleus surrounded by a cloud of negatively charged electrons spinning at a great distance, making the atom neutral. Electrons have very little mass, so although the nucleus is less than one ten-thousandth the size of the atom it holds more than 99.9% of its mass. A cubic centimetre of nucleus material would weigh 100 million tonnes (not tested).

fields.Front: What is in the nucleus and what holds it together?
fields.Back: Positively charged protons and neutral neutrons, held together by the 'strong' or 'nuclear' force - a very strong force whose effectiveness drops off quickly with distance.
The progressive breakdown (decay) of the nucleus of an atom or isotope. Every unstable isotope decays at its own characteristic rate, which has never changed in all of time.

fields.Front: What kinds of decay does the reading mention, and what is the essential result?
fields.Back: Beta decay, alpha decay, fission and others - not detailed in the course. What matters is that one atom breaks down to form a new atom of a DIFFERENT element.

fields.Front: Why is radioactive decay called exponential?
fields.Back: During each half-life only half of the remaining parents become daughters, and there are fewer parents as time goes on - so the number of daughter atoms produced is large at the beginning and rapidly becomes smaller. But at each half-life the same proportion (exactly half of the remaining parent) decays.

fields.Front: Give the parent remaining after 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 half-lives.
fields.Back:
0: 100%
1: 50%
2: 25%
3: 12.5%
4: 6.25%
(after ~10 half-lives about 0.1% - unmeasurable, so no useful time information)

fields.Front: Carbon-14: daughter, half-life and useful range?
fields.Back: Nitrogen-14 (per the slides); half-life 5730 years. Used for organic material younger than about 50,000 years; after about 10 half-lives (~57,000 years) all the C-14 is gone and you can only say the item is older than that.

fields.Front: If three isotope systems are analysed in one granite, what result is expected, and why is only one used in practice?
fields.Back: All three should give the same age for the sample. In practice only one technique is used because analytical costs are high.

fields.Front: Why does carbon-14 dating work on once-living things?
fields.Back: All living things take in carbon, including C-14. Once the organism dies it no longer consumes C-14 and the total amount starts to decrease by decay, so the remaining fraction gives the time since death.

fields.Front: Compare relative and absolute age dating.
fields.Back:
Relative (Steno, Hutton, Smith): orders events older/younger, works on sedimentary sequences even with recycled grains, but gives no numbers.
Absolute (radioactivity, half-lives): gives numerical ages for igneous rocks and organic matter, but needs measurable parent:daughter ratios and a closed system.
Both are still useful, and in practice they are combined.

fields.Front: How did the geologic time scale get its numbers?
fields.Back: By applying radiometric dating to rocks around the world, producing numerical ages for each major boundary of the stratigraphic column - e.g. the two dramatic extinction events at 251 Ma and 65.5 Ma.

fields.Text: Modern absolute dating became possible in {{c1::1896}} when {{c1::Henri Becquerel}} discovered that atoms of some elements, such as {{c1::uranium}}, are inherently unstable and break down predictably - the property called {{c1::radioactivity}}.

Atomic number = the number of {{c1::protons}}, the same for every atom of an element; atomic mass = protons plus {{c1::neutrons}}. (The reading labels atomic number {{c1::A}} and atomic mass {{c1::Z}}.)

{{c1::Isotopes}} are atoms of the same element that differ in the number of {{c1::neutrons}} in the nucleus and thus in {{c1::mass}}; they behave the same {{c1::chemically}}, though heavier ones react slightly more slowly.

Hydrogen has three isotopes: mass 1 (1 proton, 0 neutrons, {{c1::stable}}), mass 2 (1 proton, 1 neutron, {{c1::stable}}) and mass {{c1::3}} (1 proton, {{c1::2}} neutrons), which is {{c1::radioactive}}.
The original isotope in any step of a decay is the {{c1::parent}}; the isotope produced by that step, an atom of a {{c1::different element}}, is the {{c1::daughter}}.

The {{c1::half-life}} is the period of time in which exactly {{c1::half}} the nuclei of a radioactive species decay, in any step of the breakdown. Measuring a changing {{c1::fraction}} is far easier than measuring absolute quantities.

At time zero a rock has {{c1::100%}} parent; after 1 half-life the parent:daughter ratio is {{c1::50:50}}; after 2 half-lives {{c1::25:75}}; after about {{c1::10}} half-lives the parent is too small for our instruments to measure.
Half-lives: U-235 = {{c1::704 million}} years; K-40 = {{c1::1.26 billion}} years; Rb-87 = {{c1::48.8 billion}} years; C-14 = {{c1::5730}} years.
{{c1::Zircon}} is the mineral sought for dating igneous rocks because it contains {{c1::uranium}}; the {{c1::uranium:lead}} ratio in the crystal gives its age.
A {{c1::closed system}} is a rock or mineral that has neither gained nor lost {{c1::parent or daughter}} atoms since it formed, so the ratio reflects only {{c1::elapsed time}}.
